rule: 'Bestowed' means gave or granted. The inspector now looks at the butler with 'closer attention' than he had given him before.

s: No place for anyone to hide here, thought Tuppence, with a sigh of relief, then chided herself indignantly.

definitions.ensconced: settled snugly and securely in a place
definitions.ingratiated: won favor by being pleasing to someone

rule: 'Chided' means scolded. She feels relief and then scolds herself, and the word 'indignantly' shows she was annoyed with herself.

s: We will concoct a business like letter to the Ambassador, informing him that the matter has been dealt with satisfactorily.

definitions.concoct: invent or put together, often cleverly
definitions.brandish: wave around in a threatening or showy way

rule: 'Concoct' means to invent or put together. They plan a letter 'informing him that the matter has been dealt with', so they are making it up themselves.

s: Poirot deigned to attend to me for a brief moment.

definitions.deigned: agreed to do something as if beneath oneself
definitions.contrived: managed to do something by clever planning
definitions.endeavored: made a serious effort to do something
definitions.presumed: dared to do something without having the right

rule: 'Deigned' means did something as if it were a favor beneath oneself. Poirot gave the narrator only 'a brief moment', which shows his grudging attitude.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: I desisted at last, and either fainted or fell asleep.

definitions.desisted: stopped doing something; gave up the effort
definitions.vacillated: wavered between choices; could not decide
definitions.retaliated: struck back in return for harm

rule: 'Desisted' means stopped doing something. After this the speaker 'either fainted or fell asleep', so the effort or struggle had ended.

s: Poirot threw a withering glance at me, which I knew enjoined me to keep my mouth shut.

definitions.enjoined: ordered or strongly urged someone to do something

rule: 'Enjoined' means ordered or strongly urged. A 'withering glance' that tells him to 'keep my mouth shut' is a silent command.

s: I shall eschew the 'Mustard and Cress' in future.

definitions.eschew: deliberately avoid or keep away from
definitions.deplore: strongly feel or say something is wrong

rule: 'Eschew' means to avoid on purpose. 'In future' shows he plans to stay away from the 'Mustard and Cress'.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: To begin with, he alluded to my exalted position and importance and suggested that I should remove myself, or be removed by him, to Pretoria.

definitions.exalted: raised high in rank, power, or dignity
definitions.precarious: unsteady and likely to fail or fall
definitions.ostensible: seeming to be so, though perhaps not truly
definitions.ambiguous: open to more than one meaning

rule: 'Exalted' means very high in rank or importance. It is paired with 'importance' to describe a high position.

s: I followed John’s example, and went out into the hall, where Miss Howard was endeavouring to extricate herself from the voluminous mass of veils that enveloped her head.

definitions.extricate: free from a tangle or trap
definitions.absolve: declare free from blame or guilt
definitions.insulate: protect from harm or outside effects

rule: 'Extricate' means to free from something tangled or trapping. She struggles with 'a voluminous mass of veils', so she is trying to get loose from them.

s: Mrs. Howell was only too willing to talk about it, and was full of pitying ejaculations about the poor young gentleman, but Bundle gleaned nothing new.

definitions.gleaned: gathered information slowly in small bits

rule: 'Gleaned' means gathered bit by bit. Bundle listens to Mrs. Howell talk but 'gleaned nothing new', meaning she picked up no new information.

s: She had been guilty of much, but she was innocent of the terrible crime imputed to her.

definitions.imputed: blamed on someone; credited to a person as the cause
definitions.bequeathed: left to someone in a will
definitions.relegated: moved to a lower or less important position

rule: 'Imputed' means blamed on or credited to someone. She was guilty of 'much' but innocent of the terrible crime that was pinned on her.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: I walked out with what dignity I could muster.

definitions.relinquish: give up or let go of

rule: 'Muster' means to gather up or summon. He walks out with as much dignity as he could pull together.

s: A fourth or super-theory was propounded by Caroline later as we went up to bed.

definitions.propounded: put forward an idea for consideration
definitions.deciphered: figured out the meaning of something unclear
definitions.relinquished: gave up or let go of

rule: 'Propounded' means put forward for consideration. Caroline offers 'a fourth' theory, a new idea added to the earlier ones.

s: Evidently the incident of the pound note still rankled.

definitions.tantalized: teased by offering what is out of reach

rule: 'Rankled' means caused lasting resentment. The word 'still' shows the annoyance over the 'pound note' had not faded.

s: Still, he reiterated the fact, he had had a very good life.

definitions.embellished: decorated with extra, often untrue, details

rule: 'Reiterated' means said again. He keeps repeating the fact that he 'had had a very good life'.

s: The date stipulated upon for delivering the manuscript was a little over a week ahead.

definitions.stipulated: specified as a required condition of an agreement
definitions.ruminated: thought about something deeply for a long time

rule: 'Stipulated' means specified as part of an agreement. It is the date agreed on 'for delivering the manuscript'.

s: She rang off in a tantalizing manner which left Jimmy pleasantly puzzled.

definitions.tantalizing: teasing by offering what is just out of reach
definitions.unnerving: making someone feel nervous or shaken

rule: 'Tantalizing' means teasing by offering something and then holding it back. She 'rang off' and left Jimmy 'pleasantly puzzled', so she teased him with too little information.

why: only candidate says Apaches were hired to waylay you, using an outdated gang label that reads as a Native American group name; unsuitable and confusing out of context

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: He had displayed the greatest antipathy to me from the first.

definitions.antipathy: strong dislike or hostility toward someone
definitions.deference: polite respect for another's wishes or status
definitions.allegiance: loyalty to a person, group, or cause
definitions.condescension: behavior that treats others as inferior

rule: 'Antipathy' means strong dislike. The sentence says he showed it 'from the first', aimed at the narrator.

s: Poirot replied seriously to the other’s banter.

definitions.reproof: a mild scolding for a fault
definitions.innuendo: an indirect hint, often suggesting something unpleasant

rule: 'Banter' means light, joking talk. Poirot 'replied seriously', which contrasts with the playful tone of the other person.

s: There was a good deal of this before we came to the point, and even then it was approached with a good deal of circumlocution.

definitions.circumlocution: using many words to avoid getting to the point
definitions.trepidation: nervous fear about what may happen
definitions.subterfuge: a sneaky trick used to hide the truth
definitions.deference: polite respect for another's wishes or status

rule: 'Circumlocution' means talking around a subject in a roundabout way. It took a long time 'before we came to the point'.

s: The American is a connoisseur, the things are genuine and beautiful, some of them beyond price.

definitions.connoisseur: an expert judge of art or fine things
definitions.recluse: a person who lives alone, avoiding others
definitions.emissary: a person sent to represent another on a mission

rule: 'Connoisseur' means an expert judge of fine things. The man owns objects that are 'genuine and beautiful', so he clearly knows art well.

s: After that, I placed very little credence in her statements.

definitions.credence: belief in something as true; trust
definitions.deference: polite respect for another's wishes or status
definitions.trepidation: nervous fear about what may happen

rule: 'Credence' means belief or trust. 'After that' shows something made him doubt her, so he trusted 'her statements' very little.

s: She had judged him as an elderly dilettante, easily flattered by a pretty woman.

definitions.dilettante: someone who dabbles in a subject without serious commitment
definitions.sycophant: a person who flatters important people to gain favor
definitions.malcontent: a person always unhappy and complaining

rule: 'Dilettante' means someone who dabbles in the arts without serious commitment. She sees him as an elderly man who is 'easily flattered', not a true expert.

s: Poirot, however, did not seem grateful to me for my forbearance.

definitions.levity: light, joking behavior in a serious moment

rule: 'Forbearance' means patient restraint. The narrator held back, yet 'Poirot did not seem grateful' for it.

s: It was at this juncture that Tommy lost his head.

definitions.juncture: a particular point in time, often a critical one
definitions.impasse: a deadlock where no progress is possible
definitions.contretemps: an awkward, unexpected mishap or disagreement

rule: 'Juncture' means a particular point in time, especially an important one. 'At this juncture' means at this moment in events.

why: nothing in the sentence shows she is lying, so several positive nouns would fit equally well and the answer cannot be worked out from context

s: At last he found the missive, and handed it to Poirot.

definitions.decoy: something used to lure into a trap
definitions.heirloom: a valuable object passed down in a family
definitions.talisman: an object believed to bring luck or protection

rule: 'Missive' means a letter or written message. Someone searches for it and hands it to Poirot to read.

s: Into this pandemonium stepped Poirot, neat and smiling.

definitions.coterie: a small, exclusive group of friends
definitions.milieu: a person's social surroundings or setting
definitions.quandary: a state of not knowing what to do

rule: 'Pandemonium' means wild, noisy chaos. Poirot steps in 'neat and smiling', which contrasts with the disorder around him.

s: Mrs. Inglethorp reads it, and becomes aware of the perfidy of her husband and Evelyn Howard, though, unfortunately, the sentence about the bromides conveys no warning to her mind.

definitions.affluence: wealth; a plentiful supply of money

rule: 'Perfidy' means treachery or betrayal of trust. She learns something shocking about 'her husband and Evelyn Howard' from what she reads.

book: The Mystery of the Blue Train
s: Some quick rejoinder was springing to Derek's lips, but he checked it as though something in the little Belgian's twinkling eyes had made him suddenly alert.
rule: 'Rejoinder' means a quick reply. It is something 'springing to Derek's lips', words he is about to say back.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: I took advantage of the respite to open my bag and powder my nose thoroughly.

definitions.respite: a short break from something hard or unpleasant
definitions.pretext: a false reason given to hide the real one
definitions.tirade: a long, angry speech of criticism

rule: 'Respite' means a short break from something hard. She uses the pause to open her bag and powder her nose.

s: Suddenly it widened out into a little clearing, which showed signs of recent upheaval.

definitions.upheaval: a violent disturbance or sudden upsetting change
definitions.habitation: the act of living in a place

rule: 'Upheaval' means a violent disturbance or heaving up. The clearing shows 'signs of recent' disturbance, as if the ground had been dug up.

s: She spoke of Buda Pesth shortly after the war and traced its vicissitudes to the present day.

definitions.vicissitudes: unwelcome changes of fortune; ups and downs
definitions.anachronisms: things placed in the wrong time period
definitions.paradoxes: statements that seem to contradict themselves yet may be true

rule: 'Vicissitudes' means ups and downs, or changes of fortune. A history of a city 'traced' to the present day would follow its changing fortunes.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: An ardent anthropologist himself, he was a great admirer of Papa’s works.

definitions.ardent: passionately enthusiastic and devoted to something
definitions.austere: strict, severe, and plain, with no luxury

rule: 'Ardent' means passionately enthusiastic. He is an anthropologist 'himself' and a 'great admirer' of Papa's works, so he shares that devotion.

s: When he arrived it was in his most cantankerous mood.

definitions.cantankerous: bad tempered, argumentative, and hard to please
definitions.lugubrious: gloomy and mournful, often in an exaggerated way
definitions.complacent: smugly satisfied and unaware of any danger
definitions.obsequious: overly eager to please or obey

rule: 'Cantankerous' means grumpy and quarrelsome. A person can arrive in a 'mood', and 'most cantankerous' means his bad temper was at its worst.

s: John practised for some time as a barrister, but had finally settled down to the more congenial life of a country squire.

definitions.congenial: pleasant because it suits one's tastes and personality
definitions.precarious: dangerously uncertain or likely to fall apart
definitions.ephemeral: lasting only a very short time
definitions.ostentatious: showy in a way meant to impress others

rule: 'Congenial' means pleasantly suited to a person's tastes. John 'finally settled down' to country life after law, which shows it suited him better.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: I knew that he had taken an interest in the case and was conversant with all the details.

definitions.conversant: well informed about and familiar with a subject
definitions.complacent: smugly satisfied and unaware of any danger
definitions.contrite: feeling sorry and guilty for having done wrong

rule: Being 'conversant' with something means knowing it well. He 'had taken an interest in the case', so he knew 'all the details'.

s: Geoffrey Raymond was fresh and debonair as ever.

definitions.debonair: charming, stylish, and relaxed in manner
definitions.lugubrious: gloomy and mournful, often in an exaggerated way

rule: 'Debonair' means charming, stylish, and carefree. It sits beside 'fresh' and 'as ever' to describe his polished, lively manner.

s: His words gave Tuppence an extraordinarily desolate feeling.

definitions.ephemeral: lasting only a very short time
definitions.palpable: so strong that it can almost be felt
definitions.frivolous: silly and not serious about important matters

rule: 'Desolate' means bleak and lonely. It describes the empty, hopeless 'feeling' that his words gave Tuppence.

s: The subject was a disconsolate and somewhat misshapen young woman weeping over an urn.

definitions.disconsolate: deeply unhappy and impossible to cheer up
definitions.haughty: arrogantly proud and looking down on others
definitions.garrulous: talking too much about unimportant things
definitions.petulant: sulky and bad tempered over small things

rule: 'Disconsolate' means deeply unhappy and beyond comfort. The woman is 'weeping over an urn', which shows her grief.

s: He had foreseen Virginia as a willing, docile tool, receiving his hints gratefully, and asking no awkward questions.

definitions.docile: gentle, obedient, and easy to control
definitions.unscrupulous: willing to act dishonestly with no moral limits
definitions.dogmatic: stubbornly insisting that one's opinions are certainly right
definitions.garish: unpleasantly bright and flashy in color

rule: 'Docile' means obedient and easy to control. He expected her to take his hints 'gratefully' and ask 'no awkward questions', like a willing tool.

s: I suspected at first that some one was impersonating Prince Michael, but that proved to be a totally erroneous idea.

definitions.pertinent: directly relevant to the matter at hand

rule: 'Erroneous' means wrong or mistaken. The word 'but' and the phrase 'proved to be' show that his first suspicion turned out to be false.

s: His laugh sounded a little fatuous to Mr. Satterthwaite, and no responsive smile came to the girl's face.

definitions.fatuous: foolish and smug in a pointless way
definitions.surreptitious: done secretly to avoid being noticed

rule: 'Fatuous' means silly and self satisfied. His laugh struck Mr. Satterthwaite as foolish, and 'no responsive smile' came from the girl.

s: He thinks every death that takes place here must necessarily be a case of foul play fraught with grave political significance.

definitions.fraught: filled with something, usually trouble or danger
definitions.incongruous: out of place and not fitting with surroundings
definitions.conversant: well informed about and familiar with a subject

rule: 'Fraught with' means filled with. He believes each death must be foul play loaded with 'grave political significance'.

why: Only candidate uses it to describe a smirk, a stretched use with no context clue to the meaning.

s: After many harrowing experiences she finally marries the man she loves.

definitions.harrowing: extremely distressing and painful to go through
definitions.exemplary: so good that it serves as a model
definitions.rudimentary: basic and undeveloped, at a simple level

rule: 'Harrowing' means extremely distressing. She endures hardship before she 'finally' marries the man she loves, so the experiences were painful.

s: At least a dozen impecunious young men were to be found dangling around her on all occasions, in the hunting-field, in the ballroom, wherever she went.

definitions.precocious: unusually mature or skilled for one's age

rule: 'Impecunious' means having very little money. It describes the dozen young men who hang around her wherever she goes.

s: She swore that she had only been indiscreet, and I believe her.

definitions.indiscreet: careless about what one says or does
definitions.morose: gloomy, sullen, and unwilling to talk
definitions.capricious: changing mood or behavior suddenly without reason

rule: 'Indiscreet' means unwise or careless about what you say or do. She swears she was 'only' this, meaning careless rather than truly guilty.

s: And here it was that the innate weakness of Ralph Paton showed itself.

definitions.innate: present from birth; natural rather than learned
definitions.superficial: shallow and only on the surface
definitions.ominous: suggesting that something bad is coming

rule: 'Innate' means inborn. His weakness 'showed itself' at this moment, which suggests it was part of his nature all along.

s: Anthony, who had been standing, irresolute, sat down again.

definitions.irresolute: unable to make up one's mind; hesitant
definitions.oblivious: completely unaware of what is happening around one
definitions.jaunty: cheerful, lively, and full of self confidence

rule: 'Irresolute' means undecided. Anthony stood around and then 'sat down again', which fits someone who cannot decide what to do.

s: Renauld was a man of medium height, slender and lithe in figure.

definitions.lithe: flexible, graceful, and quick in movement
definitions.formidable: inspiring fear or respect through size or power
definitions.stolid: calm and showing little emotion or excitement
definitions.tawdry: cheap, showy, and of poor quality

rule: 'Lithe' means slim, flexible, and graceful. It is paired with 'slender' to describe the shape of his body.

s: Poirot was alternately silent and loquacious.

definitions.loquacious: tending to talk a great deal
definitions.fastidious: very fussy about details and cleanliness

rule: 'Loquacious' means talkative. It is set against 'silent', since he switched between the two.

s: Evidently something very momentous had occurred that afternoon.

definitions.momentous: of great importance, with serious consequences
definitions.ludicrous: so silly that it is laughable
definitions.furtive: secretive and trying not to be noticed

rule: 'Momentous' means very important. 'Evidently something very' big 'had occurred' tells you a major event had happened that afternoon.

s: He was now sitting up in bed, propped up with pillows, his head muffled in a woollen shawl, and was slowly sipping a particularly noxious tisane which I had prepared according to his directions.

definitions.noxious: harmful or very unpleasant to taste or smell
definitions.insipid: bland and lacking flavor or interest
definitions.venerable: respected because of great age or wisdom

rule: 'Noxious' means harmful or foul. He sips the drink 'slowly' while sick in bed, which suggests it tastes unpleasant.

s: I can assure you that Madame Colombier’s is a most high-class and orthodox establishment.

definitions.clandestine: kept secret, often because it is not allowed
definitions.boisterous: noisy, rowdy, and full of rough energy
definitions.dilapidated: falling apart because of age or neglect

rule: 'Orthodox' means conventional and proper. The speaker says 'I can assure you' to reassure the listener that the place is respectable.

s: In another minute they were being introduced to Mrs. Kingston Bruce, a plaintive lady with a languid manner.

definitions.plaintive: sad and mournful, often with a whining tone
definitions.haughty: arrogantly proud and looking down on others
definitions.scrupulous: extremely careful to do what is right
definitions.shrewd: clever at judging people and situations

rule: 'Plaintive' means sad and complaining. It goes with her 'languid manner' to paint a mournful, droopy woman.

s: I was aware of my friend looking at me with a quizzical smile, the meaning of which I could not fathom.

definitions.quizzical: showing mild puzzlement or teasing curiosity
definitions.complacent: smugly satisfied and unaware of any danger
definitions.furtive: secretive and trying not to be noticed
definitions.jaunty: cheerful, lively, and full of self confidence

rule: 'Quizzical' means questioning in a puzzled or teasing way. His smile seemed to ask something, and the narrator could not 'fathom' its meaning.

s: So I say again we have been strangely remiss.

definitions.remiss: careless about doing what one should
definitions.garrulous: talking too much about unimportant things
definitions.dogmatic: stubbornly insisting that one's opinions are certainly right

rule: 'Remiss' means careless about a duty, failing to do what you should. 'I say again' and 'strangely' show the speaker is criticizing a lapse.

s: Tommy suspected her father, the saturnine M. Heroulade.

definitions.saturnine: gloomy, serious, and unfriendly in manner
definitions.venerable: respected because of great age or wisdom
definitions.wily: clever at getting one's way through trickery
definitions.fastidious: very fussy about details and cleanliness

rule: 'Saturnine' means gloomy and grim. It describes M. Heroulade as a dark, forbidding man, the kind Tommy would 'suspect'.

s: The staid respectability of Mr. Satterthwaite impressed her favorably.

definitions.staid: serious, sedate, and unadventurous in manner
definitions.mercurial: unpredictably changing in mood or behavior
definitions.tawdry: cheap, showy, and of poor quality
definitions.zealous: full of intense enthusiasm for a cause

rule: 'Staid' means serious, quiet, and conventional. It goes with 'respectability' to describe a steady, proper man who impressed her.

s: The voice of a butler, suave and deferential, answered him.

definitions.suave: smooth, polished, and charming in manner
definitions.stolid: calm and showing little emotion or excitement
definitions.petulant: sulky and bad tempered over small things
definitions.wary: cautious about possible danger or trouble

rule: 'Suave' means smooth and polished. It fits a butler's voice and is paired with 'deferential', which means respectful.

s: Age at a guess, twenty-five, big and rather ungainly in his movements, a pleasurably ugly face, a splendid set of white teeth and a pair of honest brown eyes.

definitions.furtive: secretive and trying not to be noticed
definitions.impetuous: acting quickly without thinking about consequences

rule: 'Ungainly' means awkward and clumsy. He is described as 'big', and the word describes how he moves.

s: He kept his hand in the pocket of his coat, but his manner was urbane to the last degree.

definitions.urbane: polished, courteous, and sophisticated in manner
definitions.truculent: eager to argue or fight; aggressively hostile
definitions.obsequious: overly eager to please or obey

rule: 'Urbane' means polished, smooth, and courteous. The word 'but' sets his hidden hand against his very polite manner.

s: A rather wistful smile passed across the face of the prisoner in the dock.

definitions.wistful: sadly longing for something out of reach
definitions.sardonic: mocking in a bitter, scornful way
definitions.complacent: smugly satisfied and unaware of any danger
definitions.perfunctory: done quickly without real interest or effort

rule: 'Wistful' means sadly longing for something. It describes the smile of a 'prisoner in the dock', who might long for freedom.

why: Used as 'abjured' to mean urged or begged (really 'adjured'), not its usual sense of renouncing.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: I decided that I would accost him then and there.

definitions.accost: approach and speak to boldly or aggressively
definitions.placate: calm someone and make them less angry
definitions.emulate: copy someone because one admires them

rule: 'Accost' means to approach someone and speak to them boldly. He decided to do it 'then and there', right away.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: By one master-stroke the blackmailed had rid himself of the blackmailer, and at the same time had provided a victim to whom the crime would be ascribed.

definitions.ascribed: credited or blamed on a particular person
definitions.relinquished: gave up or let go of
definitions.refuted: proved to be false or wrong

rule: 'Ascribed' means attributed to someone. A victim was provided so that the crime would be blamed on him.

s: The augmented syndicate established itself comfortably in the corner by the window, being grouped round a long oak table.

definitions.augmented: made larger by adding more members or parts
definitions.mollified: calmed down and made less angry
definitions.vindicated: shown to be right or innocent

rule: 'Augmented' means made larger. The group had grown, so it was 'grouped round a long oak table' as a bigger syndicate.

s: His back was much bent, though he was probably not as old as he looked, but his eyes were sharp and intelligent, and belied his slow and rather cautious speech.

definitions.belied: gave a false impression of or contradicted
definitions.lamented: expressed deep sorrow or regret about
definitions.emulated: copied because one admired and wanted to match

rule: 'Belied' means contradicted or gave a false impression. His sharp, intelligent eyes did not match his 'slow and rather cautious speech'.

s: He drew a revolver from his pocket and brandished it in the air.

definitions.brandished: waved about in a showy or threatening way
definitions.relinquished: gave up or let go of
definitions.extricated: freed from a difficult or tight situation

rule: 'Brandished' means waved about in a showy or threatening way. He took out a revolver and did it 'in the air'.

s: He sought rapidly in his mind for the best way of circumventing her without overt rudeness.

definitions.circumventing: finding a way around or avoiding
definitions.emulating: copying someone because one admires them
definitions.vilifying: speaking about in a cruelly insulting way

rule: 'Circumventing' means getting around or avoiding. He wants a way past her 'without overt rudeness'.

s: She feared someone was on her track, and not daring to conceal it amongst her own belongings, she contrived this hiding-place.

definitions.contrived: cleverly devised or made through effort
definitions.eschewed: deliberately avoided or kept away from
definitions.disparaged: spoke of as being of little value

rule: 'Contrived' means cleverly devised. She did not dare hide it among her own things, so she came up with a new hiding place.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: I did not delude myself into the belief that that really meant anything.

definitions.delude: fool someone into believing something false
definitions.placate: calm someone and make them less angry
definitions.vindicate: show to be right or innocent

rule: 'Delude' means to fool or mislead. The phrase 'myself into the belief' shows he refused to trick himself into thinking it mattered.

s: Called in professionally to elucidate the mystery of a stolen pearl necklace at Adlington Hall, Adlington, Blunt's Brilliant Detectives had failed to make good.

definitions.lament: express deep sorrow or regret about
definitions.relinquish: give up or let go of

rule: 'Elucidate' means make clear by explaining. Detectives are called in to explain the 'mystery' of a stolen necklace, and these ones 'had failed'.

s: But at that moment two elderly ladies rose and collected parcels, and Tuppence deftly ensconced herself in one of the vacant seats.

definitions.ensconced: settled snugly and comfortably into a place
definitions.extricated: freed from a difficult or tight situation
definitions.vindicated: shown to be right or innocent
definitions.mollified: calmed down and made less angry

rule: 'Ensconced' means settled snugly into a place. Two ladies left their seats, and Tuppence quickly took 'one of the vacant seats'.

why: Used in the old sense of 'married', not the usual modern sense of supporting a cause.

s: I was about to expound these theories to Poirot, when his own words distracted me.

definitions.expound: explain in detail and at length
definitions.relinquish: give up or let go of

rule: 'Expound' means explain in detail. He was about to lay out his own 'theories' to Poirot when he was interrupted.

s: Ursula flushed and began to speak, but Flora forestalled her.

definitions.emulated: copied because one admired and wanted to match

rule: 'Forestalled' means stopped by acting first. Ursula 'began to speak, but' Flora got in ahead of her.

s: You are still hampered by your preconceived notion.

definitions.hampered: held back or made more difficult
definitions.perplexed: confused by something hard to understand
definitions.vindicated: shown to be right or innocent
definitions.mollified: calmed down and made less angry

rule: 'Hampered' means held back or hindered. A 'preconceived notion' gets in the way of seeing the truth, and 'still' shows it keeps holding him back.

s: Strangely enough my words only seemed to incense her further.

definitions.perplex: confuse with something hard to understand
definitions.beguile: charm or enchant, sometimes by trickery
definitions.placate: calm someone and make them less angry

rule: 'Incense' means make very angry. 'Only' and 'further' show her feeling grew worse, and 'strangely enough' says he did not expect that.

book: The Mystery of the Blue Train
s: A feeling of intense uneasiness pervaded her and grew stronger moment by moment.

definitions.beguiled: charmed or enchanted, sometimes by trickery

rule: 'Pervaded' means spread through and filled. The uneasiness filled her and 'grew stronger moment by moment'.

book: The Mystery of the Blue Train
s: It purported to deal with a missing scarf-pin, and was addressed to Inspector Japp, Scotland Yard.

definitions.purported: claimed to be something, whether true or not
definitions.deigned: did something one thinks is beneath one's dignity
definitions.contrived: cleverly devised or made through effort
definitions.connived: secretly cooperated in a plot or wrongdoing

rule: 'Purported' means claimed or seemed to be. The letter claimed 'to deal with' a missing pin.

s: Turning into a photographer's and demanding a few assorted photographs, they were met with a cold rebuff.

definitions.respite: a short break from something difficult

rule: A 'rebuff' is a blunt rejection. Being 'met with a cold' one means they were turned away unkindly.

s: My sister immediately reproved me for clumsiness, but half-heartedly.

definitions.regaled: entertained with stories or amusing talk
definitions.waylaid: stopped suddenly in order to attack or delay

rule: 'Reproved' means scolded. She scolded him 'for clumsiness', though only mildly.

why: Used to mean sinking or settling into chairs, not the usual 'die down' sense.

s: It was possible that something had transpired in that interview which would throw light upon the problem of his murder.
rule: 'Transpired' here means happened. Something that took place 'in that interview' might explain the murder.

s: A musical comedy chorus of brigands rushed aboard and wrested hand luggage from the passengers by main force.

definitions.bestowed: gave as an honor or gift
definitions.extricated: freed from a difficult or tight situation

rule: 'Wrested' means pulled away by force. The brigands took luggage 'from the passengers by main force'.

s: He dashed energetically in pursuit of the shadowy apparition.

definitions.apparition: a ghostly figure or strange sudden appearance
definitions.emissary: a person sent on a mission as a representative
definitions.milieu: the social surroundings in which one lives
definitions.penchant: a strong liking or habit for something

rule: An 'apparition' is a ghostly figure or strange sudden appearance. He chased something 'shadowy' that he glimpsed.

s: I felt a cold sinking, as though some unutterable calamity had befallen me.

definitions.calamity: a sudden disaster causing great damage or distress
definitions.inkling: a slight hint or vague idea

rule: A 'calamity' is a terrible disaster. The 'cold sinking' feeling is what you would feel if something awful had 'befallen' you.

s: But now that those letters have been definitely proved to have nothing whatever to do with her, any idea of her complicity becomes absurd.

definitions.complicity: involvement in a crime or wrongdoing
definitions.forbearance: patient self control, especially when provoked
definitions.demeanor: a person's outward manner and behavior
definitions.levity: lack of seriousness about serious matters

rule: 'Complicity' means involvement in wrongdoing. The letters have 'nothing whatever to do with her', so thinking she took part is absurd.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: But for these small contretemps, all had been going smoothly.

definitions.penchants: strong likings or habits for something

rule: A 'contretemps' is a small, awkward mishap. The sentence says that 'but for' them, everything went 'smoothly'.

s: You would be used as a decoy to get the great Hercule Poirot into their clutches.

definitions.decoy: bait used to lure someone into a trap
definitions.paragon: a perfect example of a quality
definitions.sycophant: a person who flatters the powerful to gain favor
definitions.dilettante: someone who dabbles in a subject without serious commitment

rule: A 'decoy' is bait used to lure someone into a trap. You would be used 'to get' Poirot 'into their clutches'.

s: Now, to begin with, there were two facts and one little discrepancy in time which especially attracted my attention.

definitions.discrepancy: a difference between things that should match
definitions.respite: a short break from something difficult
definitions.upheaval: a sudden, violent disturbance or change

rule: A 'discrepancy' is a mismatch between things that should agree. A detective would notice a small mismatch 'in time', like a timeline that does not add up.

s: After a few muttered imprecations he handed the Bradshaw to Tommy as being more conversant with its mysteries.

definitions.imprecations: angry curses spoken against someone or something
definitions.vicissitudes: unwelcome changes and ups and downs of fortune

rule: 'Imprecations' are curses. He 'muttered' them in frustration before handing the confusing timetable to Tommy.

s: I confess, my dear child, that I have in the past been disappointed by your levity.

definitions.levity: lack of seriousness about serious matters
definitions.pertinacity: stubborn persistence; refusal to give up
definitions.forbearance: patient self control, especially when provoked

rule: 'Levity' means treating serious things too lightly. He has been 'disappointed' by it, so it is a fault he is criticizing.

s: This unlucky encounter with Giraud had roused Poirot and put him on his mettle.

definitions.mettle: courage and spirit when facing a challenge
definitions.milieu: the social surroundings in which one lives
definitions.penchant: a strong liking or habit for something

rule: 'Mettle' means courage and spirit. To be put 'on his mettle' is to be pushed to do his best, and the encounter 'roused' Poirot.

s: Her husband, who had supplied her with the aforementioned children and a title, but who was otherwise a complete nonentity, had seized at the chance to escape.

definitions.nonentity: a person of no importance or influence
definitions.dilettante: someone who dabbles in a subject without serious commitment
definitions.sycophant: a person who flatters the powerful to gain favor
definitions.recluse: a person who lives alone and avoids others

rule: A 'nonentity' is a person of no importance. The husband gave her children and a title, 'but' was 'otherwise' a nobody.

s: When the police came to look into his antecedents they were confronted with a singular paucity of material.

definitions.milieu: the social surroundings in which one lives

rule: 'Paucity' means a very small amount. The police were 'confronted with' too little material about his past.

s: Gilmour Wilson had gone on challenging him with real Yankee pertinacity, and in the end he got his way.

definitions.forbearance: patient self control, especially when provoked
definitions.levity: lack of seriousness about serious matters
definitions.demeanor: a person's outward manner and behavior

rule: 'Pertinacity' means stubborn persistence. He 'had gone on challenging' and 'in the end he got his way'.

s: She allowed him to go with her in the taxi, but to all his remonstrances she addressed a deaf ear.

definitions.remonstrances: protests meant to change someone's mind
definitions.emissaries: people sent on a mission as representatives

rule: 'Remonstrances' are protests meant to change someone's mind. She 'addressed a deaf ear', meaning she ignored them.

why: Sentence has no antecedent for 'they' and gives no context to support the meaning.

s: With an effort the Russian shook off the vagary of his fancy.

definitions.vagary: an odd, unpredictable idea or whim
definitions.upheaval: a sudden, violent disturbance or change
definitions.inkling: a slight hint or vague idea

rule: A 'vagary' is an odd, unpredictable idea or whim. He 'shook off' a passing notion of his 'fancy' with an effort.

s: Tuppence coughed, and Tommy threw a baleful glare at her.

definitions.baleful: menacing, showing harmful or hostile intent
definitions.wistful: sadly longing for something out of reach
definitions.debonair: charming, stylish, and confident in manner

rule: 'Baleful' means menacing or full of ill will. A 'glare' is an angry stare, so the word describes a threatening look.

s: Lowering her head, she repeated a manœuvre of childish days, and butted their aggressor full in the capacious middle.

definitions.capacious: having a lot of room; large and roomy
definitions.gaunt: very thin and bony, looking worn out
definitions.wily: clever at cunning tricks to get one's way
definitions.vigilant: watchful and alert for possible trouble

rule: 'Capacious' means large and roomy. It describes the aggressor's 'middle', which makes a big target for a head butt.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: For years I’ve had an instinct that it would be wise to get rid of Pagett, but the fellow was so hard-working and conscientious that I honestly couldn’t find an excuse for sacking him.

definitions.conscientious: careful and thorough about doing one's duty
definitions.reticent: quiet and reluctant to share thoughts
definitions.flamboyant: showy and attention seeking in style
definitions.wary: cautious about possible danger or trouble

rule: 'Conscientious' means careful and dutiful about work. It is paired with 'hard working', which is why he could find no excuse to fire him.

book: The Mystery of the Blue Train
s: She stole a covert glance at the figure opposite.

definitions.covert: hidden or secret, not done openly
definitions.supercilious: looking down on others with haughty scorn
definitions.jovial: cheerful, friendly, and full of good humor
definitions.quizzical: showing puzzled or mildly mocking curiosity

rule: 'Covert' means secret or hidden. To 'steal' a glance is to look without being noticed.

s: Therefore, why not wait in ambush for Conrad behind the door, and when he entered bring down a chair, or one of the decrepit pictures, smartly on to his head.

definitions.decrepit: worn out and falling apart from age
definitions.ostentatious: showy in a way meant to impress

rule: 'Decrepit' means old, worn out, and falling apart. Tuppence pictures smashing one over a man's head, which suits battered old pictures.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: We made desultory conversation for some time.

definitions.desultory: casual and aimless, without real purpose or energy

rule: 'Desultory' means aimless and halfhearted. Doing it just to 'make conversation for some time' suggests casual small talk with no real direction.

s: He now felt that Tuppence was all that was noble and disinterested.

definitions.disinterested: unselfish, not acting for personal gain
definitions.pretentious: trying to seem more important than one is

rule: 'Disinterested' means free from selfish motives. It is paired with 'noble', so it praises Tuppence for acting unselfishly. It does not mean bored.

s: He turned his earnest gaze upon me reproachfully.

definitions.earnest: serious and sincere in feeling or purpose
definitions.vacuous: empty, showing no thought or intelligence
definitions.sardonic: mocking in a bitter, scornful way

rule: 'Earnest' means serious and sincere. A gaze that is 'reproachful' shows he means his disapproval seriously, not as a joke.

s: A most estimable woman with a brilliant brain.

definitions.fastidious: very hard to please, fussy about details

rule: 'Estimable' means worthy of respect. The next phrase, 'a brilliant brain', adds to the praise.

s: Jack Renauld was sleeping an uneasy fitful sleep, his head turning from side to side, and his face still unduly flushed.

definitions.fitful: stopping and starting; restless and irregular
definitions.profound: very deep, going far below the surface
definitions.ephemeral: lasting only a very short time

rule: 'Fitful' means in fits and starts, not steady. The word 'uneasy' and his head 'turning from side to side' show broken, restless sleep.

s: I found Poirot established in an arm-chair by the fire in a garish, silk dressing-gown.

definitions.capacious: having a lot of room; large and roomy

rule: 'Garish' means too bright and flashy. It describes the 'silk' dressing gown that stands out to the narrator.

s: I did not, of course, know at the time that the will in question had only been made this afternoon, and I will admit that, when I learnt that fact, I fell into a grievous error.

definitions.grievous: very serious and causing great harm or pain
definitions.gratuitous: uncalled for and without good reason
definitions.ludicrous: so foolish or absurd it is laughable

rule: 'Grievous' means very serious. The speaker 'will admit' the mistake, which shows he sees it as a serious error.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: I went right up to the boat deck, which I believe is a heinous offence, but I decided to dare something in the cause of solitude.
rule: 'Heinous' means shockingly evil. The narrator is joking, calling a trip to the boat deck a terrible crime, which is why he says he 'decided to dare' it.

s: Anthony watched, with a good deal of enjoyment, George’s face turning slowly purple, his eyes bulging, and all the incipient symptoms of apoplexy.

definitions.incipient: just beginning to appear; in an early stage
definitions.ostensible: appearing to be true but perhaps not
definitions.ominous: suggesting something bad is about to happen

rule: 'Incipient' means just beginning. George's face is only 'turning slowly purple', so the symptoms are starting, not yet at full strength.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: Muffled in coats and rugs, and weak as a kitten on my legs, I was hauled up and deposited, an inert mass, on a deck-chair.

definitions.opaque: not letting light through; hard to see through
definitions.ominous: suggesting something bad is about to happen
definitions.unwieldy: awkward to carry or handle because of size

rule: 'Inert' means not moving. The narrator is 'weak as a kitten' and has to be 'hauled up and deposited', so he is limp and motionless.

s: There was a long pause, a pause that seemed interminable, and still those two facing each other across the table looked and looked.

definitions.interminable: seeming to go on forever; endless
definitions.poignant: deeply moving, causing sadness or sympathy
definitions.portentous: warning of something important or ominous to come
definitions.ephemeral: lasting only a very short time

rule: 'Interminable' means seeming endless. The sentence already says 'a long pause', and the word shows it felt like it would never end.

s: There was a tinge of latent resentment in his voice.

definitions.latent: present but hidden, not yet fully showing
definitions.gratuitous: uncalled for and without good reason

rule: 'Latent' means hidden but present. A mere 'tinge' of resentment is only a faint trace under the surface of his voice.

why: Used here for pale or ashen from terror, not the usual modern sense of furiously angry.

s: It was a somewhat lurid article, written with an eye to picturesque effect.

definitions.lurid: shocking and sensational, meant to startle
definitions.cursory: quick and hasty, without much care

rule: 'Lurid' means sensational and shocking. The article was 'written with an eye to picturesque effect', so it aimed to grab attention with drama.

s: Mr. Quin smiled, and a stained-glass panel behind him invested him for just a moment in a motley garment of colored light.

definitions.motley: made of many different colors; varied and mixed
definitions.nondescript: lacking any special or distinctive features

rule: 'Motley' means made up of many colors. The 'stained glass' and 'colored light' show the garment is a patchwork of different hues.

s: A successful Slack would, I thought, be even more odious than a baffled one.

definitions.formidable: inspiring fear or respect because of strength
definitions.pretentious: acting more important or cultured than one is
definitions.volatile: likely to change suddenly or explode

rule: 'Odious' means deeply unpleasant. Saying a successful Slack would be 'even more' so than a baffled one shows the narrator already finds him hard to bear.

s: King Victor’s headquarters seem to be in a parlous condition.

definitions.parlous: dangerous and uncertain; full of risk
definitions.dilapidated: falling apart through age or neglect

rule: 'Parlous' means dangerous or risky. It describes the 'condition' of King Victor's headquarters, which 'seem to be' in real trouble.

s: It was proved beyond doubt that Jeanne Beroldy’s parents were a highly respectable and prosaic couple, fruit merchants, who lived on the outskirts of Lyons.

definitions.parsimonious: extremely unwilling to spend money; stingy
definitions.gregarious: sociable, enjoying the company of others

rule: 'Prosaic' means ordinary and unimaginative. It is paired with 'highly respectable', and the couple are plain fruit merchants on the 'outskirts'.

s: For the next five minutes the shop was hideous with the loud raucous ringing of many alarum clocks.

definitions.incessant: never stopping; continuing without a pause
definitions.lugubrious: gloomy and mournful, often in an exaggerated way

rule: 'Raucous' means harsh and noisy. The clocks' 'loud' ringing makes the shop 'hideous', which shows an unpleasant racket.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: They had some trouble in doing so, as the mules were very restive, but at last they managed it, and a start was made.

definitions.restive: restless and fidgety; hard to keep still
definitions.voracious: having a huge appetite; eager to consume

rule: 'Restive' means restless and hard to control. The men 'had some trouble' with the mules, which fits animals that fidget and will not stand calmly.

s: It seemed to me the most unlikely thing in the world that Lettice Protheroe should go out of her way to interfere in our domestic affairs and reprove our maid for slovenly housework.

definitions.fastidious: very fussy about neatness and details
definitions.erratic: unpredictable and not following a steady pattern

rule: 'Slovenly' means careless and untidy. People are 'reproved' for work done badly, so the housework must have been sloppy.

s: The stalwart Spanish girl met him in the passage and opened a side door for him, staring curiously at him the while.

definitions.haggard: looking worn out and tired from worry

rule: 'Stalwart' means strong and sturdy. It describes the girl's solid build as she meets him in the passage and opens the door.

s: As he entered the sumptuous apartment in which he transacted affairs of State, there was a scuffling sound.

definitions.austere: plain and severe, with no comforts
definitions.venerable: respected because of great age or wisdom
definitions.clandestine: kept secret, often because it is not allowed

rule: 'Sumptuous' means lavish and luxurious. It describes the grand room where he handles 'affairs of State'.

s: Moving in his usual unobtrusive manner, Hector Blunt came between her and the inspector.

definitions.unobtrusive: quiet and not drawing attention to oneself
definitions.officious: annoyingly eager to give orders or help

rule: 'Unobtrusive' means not drawing attention. He 'came between' them quietly, in his 'usual' way, without making a fuss.

s: Yet that evening, as she sat in front of her bedroom fire, a slim, pyjamaed figure, she found her thoughts reverting to that cheery, vacuous young man, Gerry Wade.

definitions.vacuous: empty headed; showing no intelligence or thought
definitions.garrulous: talking a lot, especially about trivial things

rule: 'Vacuous' means empty of thought. Next to 'cheery', it paints Gerry Wade as pleasant but not very thoughtful.

s: He felt suddenly rather old and out of things, a little dried-up wizened old fogey of a man.

definitions.venerable: respected because of great age or wisdom
definitions.querulous: complaining in a whining, irritable way
definitions.pedantic: overly concerned with minor rules and details

rule: 'Wizened' means shriveled and wrinkled with age. It matches the nearby phrases 'dried up' and 'old fogey'.

s: In the same way, the absconding clerk, or the domestic defaulter, is bound to be run down in these days of wireless telegraphy.

definitions.absconding: running away secretly to escape the law
definitions.conniving: secretly plotting or going along with wrongdoing
definitions.vacillating: wavering between choices; unable to decide

rule: 'Absconding' means running away secretly, often after stealing. It describes a clerk or 'defaulter' who has fled and can be 'run down'.

s: Questioned, he could adduce nothing in support of his statement except his own opinion that she wasn’t the usual kind.
rule: 'Adduce' means to cite as evidence. He had 'nothing in support of his statement' except his own opinion, so he had no proof to point to.

s: I said nothing then or at any time of the dreadful suspicion that had for one moment assailed my mind.

definitions.tantalized: teased with something desirable out of reach

rule: 'Assailed' means attacked, here by an unwelcome thought. A 'dreadful suspicion' striking his mind 'for one moment' suggests a sudden painful hit.

s: M. Renauld sent for him, but he arrived too late to do anything to avert the tragedy.
rule: 'Avert' means to prevent. He 'arrived too late', so he could do nothing to stop the tragedy.

s: The world-wide unrest, the labour troubles that beset every nation, and the revolutions that break out in some.

definitions.beset: trouble or attack from all sides
definitions.subjugate: bring under complete control by force

rule: 'Beset' means to trouble or surround with problems. The sentence names 'unrest' and 'labour troubles' hitting every nation.

s: I had been turning over an idea in my head, and I felt that the moment had now come to broach it.

definitions.broach: bring up a subject for discussion
definitions.relinquish: give up or let go of

rule: 'Broach' means to bring up a topic for the first time. He has been 'turning over an idea' and feels 'the moment had now come' to raise it.

why: Used in the idiom 'commend itself to' (appeal to), not the usual sense of praise.

book: The Mystery of the Blue Train
s: He turned on her in a rage and shouted at her, so that she cowered back before him.

definitions.subsided: sank down or became less intense
definitions.demurred: raised an objection or showed reluctance

rule: 'Cowered' means shrank away in fear. He 'turned on her in a rage and shouted', so she backed away frightened.

s: But behind them were subtle, insistent forces at work, urging the memories of old wrongs, deprecating the weakness of half-and-half measures, fomenting misunderstandings.
rule: 'Deprecating' means expressing disapproval of something. These forces are 'urging' old wrongs, so they would speak against 'measures' that only go halfway as too weak.

s: In the short space of twenty-four hours, he had become embroiled in two separate crimes.

definitions.embroiled: drawn into a difficult or troublesome situation
definitions.ensconced: settled firmly and comfortably in a place
definitions.inundated: overwhelmed by a flood of things

rule: 'Embroiled' means drawn into a messy situation. In 'the short space' of a day he has been dragged into 'two separate crimes'.

book: The Mystery of the Blue Train
s: A few brief introductory words from Poirot, and Mademoiselle Mirelle was courteously entreated to tell her tale.
rule: 'Entreated' means begged earnestly. The word 'courteously' shows polite pleading, not force.

s: Yet I found myself evincing an increasing interest in her.
rule: 'Evincing' means showing clearly. His 'increasing interest in her' is plain to see, almost against his will ('found myself').

s: A clever lawyer will make out a great case of extenuating circumstances.

definitions.extenuating: making a wrong seem less serious by giving excuses
definitions.tantalizing: teasing with something desirable out of reach

rule: 'Extenuating' means making a fault seem less serious. A lawyer builds a 'case' that excuses a crime, so these circumstances would soften the blame.

s: True enough, there he was, tearing down the street, hatless, and gesticulating as he went.

definitions.gesticulating: waving the hands and arms while speaking
definitions.cajoling: coaxing with flattery or gentle persuasion
definitions.ruminating: thinking deeply and slowly about something

rule: 'Gesticulating' means making wild hand and arm movements. He is 'tearing down the street, hatless', so he is excitedly waving his arms as he runs.

s: I wondered how he would take the exciting news I had to impart.

definitions.impart: pass on information to someone; tell
definitions.concoct: invent or make up, often a story

rule: 'Impart' means to pass on or tell. The narrator wonders how someone will react to the 'exciting news' he has to share.

s: The inspector listened keenly, occasionally interjecting a question.

definitions.interjecting: breaking in with a remark while someone else talks
definitions.circumventing: finding a way around an obstacle or rule
definitions.disparaging: speaking of as unimportant or of little value

rule: 'Interjecting' means breaking in with a remark. The inspector 'listened keenly' and spoke only 'occasionally', so his questions pop in between.

s: In another minute he was shaking hands with them both in his correct, rather prim fashion, and had accepted the shy invitation proffered him to have tea with them.
rule: 'Proffered' means offered. He 'accepted' the invitation, so it was held out to him, and 'shy' shows it was a hesitant offer.

s: Tuppence quelled him with a stern glance, and stepped inside.
rule: 'Quelled' means silenced or subdued. A 'stern glance' is enough to stop him, so she put him down with a look.

why: Sentence is confusing out of context: unclear who 'they' are and 'at the expense of' is ambiguous.

s: I was quoting, and I could see that he was not pleased with my retort.

definitions.retort: a quick, sharp reply to a remark
definitions.levity: lighthearted humor, especially when seriousness is expected
definitions.subterfuge: a sneaky trick used to hide or deceive

rule: 'Retort' means a quick, sharp reply. He was 'quoting' something back at the other man, who was 'not pleased' with that answer.

s: She paused a moment, a pink colour suffusing her cheeks.

definitions.suffusing: spreading through or over, like a color
definitions.belying: giving a false idea of; contradicting

rule: 'Suffusing' means spreading over or through. The pink 'colour' is spreading across her cheeks, as when someone blushes.

s: I had meant to upbraid him mildly for various matters, in his province, which had been muddled or shelved, but seeing his white, strained face, I felt that the man was ill.

definitions.upbraid: scold or criticize for a fault

rule: 'Upbraid' means to scold. He planned to do so 'mildly' for muddled matters, but 'seeing his white, strained face', he saw the man was ill.

s: It took but a moment for Claude to recover his aplomb.

definitions.aplomb: calm self confidence, especially under pressure
definitions.levity: lighthearted humor, especially when seriousness is expected

rule: 'Aplomb' means calm self confidence. To 'recover' it after a shock means to become steady and poised again.

s: Now Giraud laid it down as an axiom that a woman lies to save herself, the man she loves, and her child.

definitions.axiom: a statement accepted as obviously true
definitions.inkling: a slight hint or faint idea
definitions.anomaly: something that differs from what is normal

rule: 'Axiom' means a rule accepted as true. Giraud 'laid it down' as a basic principle about why women lie.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: Finally we arrived in a big clearing where on the left a path led downwards towards the chasm.

definitions.chasm: a deep, wide gap in the earth
definitions.enclave: a small area surrounded by a larger one
definitions.citadel: a fortress that guards a city

rule: 'Chasm' means a deep gap in the ground. The path led 'downwards' toward it, which suits a gorge below the clearing.

s: Suddenly glancing at her, he was seized with compunction.

definitions.compunction: a guilty feeling about having done wrong
definitions.trepidation: nervous fear about what may happen

rule: 'Compunction' means a pang of guilt or regret. He is 'seized' with it after glancing at her, so seeing her makes him feel sorry.

s: Tommy and Tuppence, young, well dressed, eager for life and with apparently money to burn, were soon made free of that particular coterie in which the Laidlaws had their being.

definitions.coterie: a small, exclusive group of friends or associates
definitions.quandary: a state of not knowing what to do
definitions.upheaval: a sudden, violent disruption or change
definitions.subterfuge: a sneaky trick used to hide or deceive

rule: 'Coterie' means a small, close circle of people. Tommy and Tuppence were 'made free of' it, meaning welcomed in.

s: Beneath his impeccable demeanor he was feeling extremely indignant.

definitions.demeanor: the way a person outwardly behaves or appears
definitions.pedigree: a person's line of ancestors; family background
definitions.subterfuge: a sneaky trick used to hide or deceive

rule: 'Demeanor' means outward behavior or manner. It is set against what he is feeling 'beneath' it, so it is the calm face he shows.

s: I was convinced that here we had an emissary of the Big Four.

definitions.emissary: a person sent on a mission as a representative
definitions.apparition: a ghostly figure or strange sudden appearance

rule: 'Emissary' means a person sent on a mission for someone else. He is called 'an emissary of the Big Four', meaning an agent sent by that group.

s: As yet I had no inkling of what that something might be.

definitions.inkling: a slight hint or faint idea
definitions.vestige: a small trace of something that once existed
definitions.precedent: an earlier example used as a guide

rule: 'Inkling' means a faint idea. 'As yet I had no' means he did not have even a hint of what the something was.

s: But there are one or two malcontents in Thurnly village, and it seemed possible that they might have had something to do with it.

definitions.malcontents: dissatisfied people who grumble or make trouble
definitions.recluses: people who live alone, avoiding others
definitions.dilettantes: people who dabble in a subject without depth

rule: 'Malcontents' means people who are discontented and troublemaking. The writer suspects them in an incident that 'might have had something to do with it'.

s: It is well to employ one's wits in a totally different milieu.

definitions.milieu: the surroundings or social setting around someone
definitions.juncture: a particular point in time or events
definitions.quandary: a state of not knowing what to do

rule: 'Milieu' means one's surroundings or setting. Using your wits in a 'totally different' one means in a new environment.

book: The Man in the Brown Suit
s: Under his tan, his face had the pallor of one who has seen a ghost.

definitions.trepidation: nervous fear about what may happen
definitions.demeanor: the way a person outwardly behaves

rule: 'Pallor' means unusual paleness. It describes his face 'under his tan', turning pale like one who 'has seen a ghost'.

s: He knew about that aspiring genius Claude Wickam, and about Lady Roscheimer, who was fat and had a penchant for young men of the artistic persuasion.

definitions.penchant: a strong liking or habit of enjoying something
definitions.disdain: scornful dislike for something thought unworthy
definitions.facility: natural ease or skill at doing something

rule: 'Penchant' means a fondness for something. The phrase 'penchant for young men of the artistic persuasion' describes a taste she is known for.

s: The prospect of her running into danger did not seem to give him any qualms whatever.

definitions.qualms: sudden doubts or pangs of conscience
definitions.respites: short breaks or rests from something hard

rule: 'Qualms' means uneasy doubts or worries. The 'prospect of her running into danger' did not bother him, so he felt no worry at all.

s: With a stern frown of reproof, the great Mr. Blunt passed into his own private office.

definitions.reproof: a criticism or scolding for a fault
definitions.trepidation: nervous fear about what may happen
definitions.compunction: a guilty feeling about doing wrong

rule: 'Reproof' means a scolding or disapproval. It goes with a 'stern frown', which is how someone shows he is displeased.

s: There was a certain bulldog tenacity about Tommy that made him slow to admit defeat.

definitions.tenacity: stubborn determination to hold on and not give up
definitions.aplomb: calm self confidence, especially under pressure

rule: 'Tenacity' means stubborn persistence. The 'bulldog' comparison and 'slow to admit defeat' show he holds on and does not quit.

book: The Mystery of the Blue Train
s: It awakened a doubt in my mind as to the general veracity of Ada Mason's statements.

definitions.levity: lighthearted humor, especially when seriousness is expected

rule: 'Veracity' means truthfulness. The 'doubt' is about whether her 'statements' can be trusted.
